name: Germinal centre
summary: A germinal centre forms inside a B-cell follicle a few days into an immune response. In the dark zone, B cells that have met their antigen divide fast and mutate their antibody genes; in the light zone they test the new antibody against antigen held by follicular dendritic cells, and the best binders win help from Tfh cells. The winners leave as plasma cells or memory B cells.
description: One germinal centre inside a B-cell follicle, as a large oval. The dark zone, packed with dividing B cells, is on the left; the light zone, with follicular dendritic cells and helper T cells, is on the right. A ring of resting B cells surrounds it, and arrows on the right show memory B cells and plasma cells leaving. Seven cells are labelled.

residents.note: Resting B cells pushed aside by the growing germinal centre form the mantle zone around it.
Divides and mutates its antibody genes in the dark zone, then moves to the light zone to be tested; it cycles between the two zones many times.
Tingible body macrophages swallow the many germinal centre B cells that die after failing selection.
Its long processes hold antigen, bound by antibody and complement, on which B cells in the light zone test their antibody.
Gives survival and division signals (CD40L, IL-21) to the B cells that show it the most antigen.
Leaves the germinal centre to recirculate, ready for a faster response next time.
Leaves the germinal centre to make high-affinity antibody, in the medulla or in the bone marrow.

regions.name: Dark zone
regions.summary: The half of the germinal centre packed with dividing B cells, which is why it looks dark in a stained tissue section. Here B cells multiply quickly while the enzyme AID mutates their antibody genes, so each daughter cell carries a slightly different antibody.
happens: Germinal centre B cells divide rapidly, several times before each round of testing.

AID puts point mutations into the genes for the antibody's binding site (somatic hypermutation), so daughter cells bind antigen more or less tightly than their parent. Many mutations make the antibody worse.
B cells whose receptor a mutation has damaged die here (shown in mice), and macrophages clear them.

CXCL12, made by reticular cells of the dark zone, holds dividing B cells here through its receptor CXCR4. After a few divisions they change to the light-zone state, seemingly on an internal timer, and move across to be tested (shown in mice).

regions.name: Light zone
regions.summary: The paler half of the germinal centre, where B cells are tested. They are less crowded here, among follicular dendritic cells that hold antigen and Tfh cells that give help. Each B cell tries to capture antigen with its mutated receptor and show it to a Tfh cell; those that capture the most survive.
happens: B cells pull antigen off the long processes of follicular dendritic cells with their mutated receptor; those whose receptor binds best take up the most.
Each B cell shows peptides from that antigen on MHC class II to Tfh cells, which give CD40L and IL-21 to the cells showing the most.
Selected B cells return to the dark zone for another round of division and mutation, or leave as plasma cells or memory B cells.
B cells that win no help die by default (in mice up to half of all germinal centre B cells die every six hours), and macrophages swallow them.
Little class switching happens here: in mice, most B cells have already switched antibody class before the germinal centre forms.
